summary:
Chubut falls under Argentina's national framework, which remains among the most permissive in the world on legal gender recognition. Law 26.743, promulgated on 24 May 2012, permits a change of legal gender without surgery, hormone treatment or judicial approval, and the United Nations described it as a pioneering step for transgender rights in the region. Argentina was also the first Latin American country to legalise marriage equality, in 2010.

That framework has been narrowed by executive action. A decree of 5 February 2025 issued by the government of President Javier Milei restricts minors' access to gender-affirming surgery and hormone therapy, and a second decree governs the housing of transgender people in prisons. Legal experts interviewed by Agencia Presentes called the measure illegal and unconstitutional and signalled an intention to seek judicial intervention.

Practical safety in the province is set by the national picture. The Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes de Odio recorded at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity in 2025, a ten-year high, up 62% year on year and averaging one every 38 hours. Perpetrators were mostly security-force personnel and unknown assailants in public space; beatings were the main modality of attack, institutional violence rose from 17 cases in 2024 to 64 in 2025, 32% of 2025 incidents occurred in police stations or prisons, and 43% of perpetrators were strangers to their victims.

Trans activists interviewed in April 2025 reported that police violence against trans and travesti sex workers has worsened since President Milei took office and is worst outside Buenos Aires, in the more conservative interior provinces. Chubut is an interior province of that description, but it has no local reporting infrastructure capable of generating separate records.

Protection machinery available to residents has weakened. Trans people hired under the 1% Trans Labor Quota were dismissed, and the federal anti-discrimination agency INADI was abolished. In April 2025 Argentina's Supreme Court left standing the life sentence imposed on Gabriel Marino for the 2015 murder of trans activist Diana Sacayán while rejecting attempts to reinstate the travesticidio aggravating circumstance removed by an appeals court in 2020, so the gender-motivated aggravation is not currently applied in that line of cases.

Outright International's country overview, updated in March 2026, records negative assessments for same-sex relations, gender recognition and the registration of civil-society organisations, an assessment of deterioration against the earlier statutory position.
tangentialFactors:
Argentina's statutory position and its day-to-day enforcement have moved in opposite directions. The country's Gender Identity Law is cited internationally as a regional model, while its hate-crime observatory registered a record year in 2025 and Outright International now rates the trajectory as one of deterioration.

Violence against LGBTIQ+ people reached a documented peak in 2025, with Agencia Presentes describing the figure as an inflection point and trans women bearing a disproportionate share of the harm. Trans activists in Buenos Aires, including representatives of organisations named for Diana Sacayán and Lohana Berkins, said the Milei government's policies had made the community more vulnerable and described the situation as chaotic and desperate.

The geographic pattern matters for a visitor's expectations. Activists locate the worst police violence against trans and travesti sex workers in interior provinces rather than the capital, which places Chubut closer to the reported epicentre of that conduct than to the more documented capital-city environment.
localsOnly:
Residents of Chubut change legal gender under Law 26.743 through an administrative procedure before the Registro del Estado Civil y Capacidad de las Personas, without surgery, hormone treatment or a court order. The same law covers the corresponding changes to the national identity document and to recorded sex on the birth certificate.

For residents, the 5 February 2025 decree limits access by minors to gender-affirming surgery and hormone therapy, and the accompanying decree governs where incarcerated transgender people are held. Legal experts interviewed by Agencia Presentes regard the minors' measure as unconstitutional and have signalled an intention to litigate.

Employment protections for trans residents rest largely on the 1% Trans Labor Quota, whose enforcement has proved fragile: trans workers hired under the quota have been dismissed. The federal anti-discrimination complaint route through INADI no longer exists following the agency's abolition, leaving residents to rely on national and provincial anti-discrimination provisions and on the courts.
outOfScopeNotes:
No local reporting infrastructure exists in Chubut to generate separate hate-crime or police-violence records, so province-level rates cannot be verified from this inventory; the figures cited are national aggregates. Whether Chubut records incidents through any provincial mechanism is unresolved.

The inventory does not source any Chubut-specific provincial statute on gender identity, hate crime or anti-discrimination beyond the national framework, so the presence or absence of a distinct provincial instrument is unresolved here.

The outcome of the legal challenges signalled against the 5 February 2025 decree is unresolved; the inventory records only the intention to seek judicial intervention and the experts' view of the decree as unconstitutional.

Whether Chubut's provincial administration complies with, or has been affected by, the Trans Labor Quota dismissals and the abolition of INADI is not sourced. The February 2025 decree's application to prisons within the province is likewise not documented in this inventory.
